title: Webhooks explained for non-developers | 50agents
description: A webhook is a message one app sends to a web address the moment something happens. What is inside one, why it arrives twice, and how to use it.
answer: A webhook is a message one app sends to a web address the moment something happens, such as a payment succeeding.
Automation tools give you the address and run your steps on each message; expect repeats and gaps.

chooser.h2: Do you need a webhook at all?

root.q: Does your automation tool have a trigger for the app?

then.why: The tool sets up the webhook with the app for you, and checks its signature. You never see the address.

options.label: No, or it is my own form

then.q: Can the app send messages to a web address?

options.label: Yes, it has a webhooks setting

then.answer: Use an automation that starts when called
then.why: It gives you an address. Paste it into the app, and each message's fields become your steps' data. Follow the steps below.
Polling asks for new records every few minutes. It is slower, and some tools count every check, even empty ones.

body.p: An app can learn what happened in another in two ways. It can keep asking "anything new?" on a timer, which is polling. Or the other app tells it the moment something happens, by posting a message to an address. That message is a webhook.

head: Polling
Webhook
rows: The other app, on an event

body.p: Inside is a small block of text, usually JSON: the event type, an event ID, the time, and the record. Your automation tool shows the fields as a list, so you never read the JSON.

steps.title: Look for a built-in trigger first
steps.body: If your tool already has "new payment" or "new order" for the app, use it. You only need your own address for apps and forms the tool does not know.

steps.title: Get an address from your tool
steps.body: Create an automation that starts when called. It gives you a web address; keep it private, because anyone who has it can post to it.

steps.title: Paste it into the sending app
steps.body: In the app's webhook settings, paste the exact address and pick only the events you need. A redirect counts as a failure at Stripe, so use the address as given.

steps.title: Send a test and map the fields
steps.body: Trigger one real event, then pick fields from the message for your steps. Stripe sends amounts in cents, so divide by 100.

steps.title: Skip repeats by ID
steps.body: Senders retry when your address does not answer fast enough: Stripe for up to 3 days, Shopify up to 8 times over 4 hours. Keep the event ID and skip ones you have done.

note.text: Events can arrive out of order too: "refunded" before "paid". Look the record up when the order matters.

steps.title: Check it is still firing
steps.body: After repeated failures, Shopify removes the webhook. If events stop, open the sending app's webhook page, and read any missed records once by hand.

captain.line: Captain sets up an automation that starts when your form posts to its address, and adds each submission as a row to your own sheet without asking.
captain.ask: Set up an automation that starts when my website form posts to it, and adds each submission as a row to my Enquiries sheet

wrong.title: Duplicate rows or emails
wrong.body: A retry ran your steps twice. Skip IDs you have already handled.

wrong.title: A slow step causes retries
wrong.body: Your address took too long to answer, so the sender tried again. Tools built for webhooks answer at once and do the work after.

wrong.title: A fake message
wrong.body: An address on the internet can receive anything. Real senders sign each message, and good tools check the signature on built-in triggers.

wrong.title: Test events mixed with real ones
wrong.body: Test mode and live mode send to the same address if you let them. Use separate addresses or check the mode field.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a webhook and an API?
faqs.a: With an API, your tool asks the app for data. With a webhook, the app sends data to your tool when something happens. Most integrations use both.
They can be: the sender signs each message, and the receiver checks the signature. A webhook address with no signature check will accept anything, so keep it private.

faqs.q: Do I need a developer to use webhooks?
faqs.a: Not with automation tools: they create and check the address for you. You need one if you are building your own endpoint.
